title: Why you should care about fiber
summary: Why 8g+ of fiber per meal matters for blood sugar and satiety, how most prepared meals fall short, and what to look for on a label.
body_markdown:
## Most people eat half the recommendation


The Recommended Dietary Allowance for fiber is 25 grams per day for women and 38 grams for men. Average intake in the United States sits at 15 to 17 grams — less than half of the recommendation for men.


The shortfall is widespread enough to be described as a public health concern, and low fiber intake has been linked to increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and certain cancers.


Unlike most nutritional gaps, this one is not contested. There is no serious argument that people are eating too much fiber.


## Fiber, fullness and blood sugar


Fiber slows digestion. That single mechanical fact drives most of its effects: food stays in the stomach longer, glucose enters the bloodstream more gradually, and the resulting blood sugar curve is flatter.


Multiple studies have found that increasing fiber intake — even without changing anything else about a diet — leads to weight loss. Not because fiber does anything exotic, but because fuller people eat less.


Soluble fiber has a second role, binding cholesterol in the gut and supporting heart health.


## Your gut microbiome runs on fiber


Fiber is not only about digestion — it is the fuel supply for gut bacteria. When fiber ferments in the colon it produces short-chain fatty acids, which reduce inflammation and help maintain the gut barrier.


A healthy microbiome has been linked to immune function, mood and metabolic health. Whatever the eventual detail of that research, the input is not in question: the bacteria need fermentable fiber, and most diets do not supply enough.


## How much fiber should you eat?


- **Active adults, or anyone aiming for optimal health:** 25–40g per day
- **Losing weight or managing blood sugar:** 30g or more, with a mix of soluble and insoluble fiber


One practical caution: increase gradually and drink more water. A sudden jump from 15g to 40g will be uncomfortable, and most people who try it conclude that fiber disagrees with them when the problem was the rate of change.


## Why protein alone does not keep you full


High-protein diets frequently fail on satiety, and fiber is usually the missing half. Protein triggers satiety signals; fiber slows the rate at which the meal empties. Together they hold for hours; separately, less so.


This is why Locale sets a floor for both rather than one: every meal carries 40–60g of protein *and* 8g or more of fiber, from colourful vegetables, beans, whole grains and leafy greens rather than isolated fiber powders. You get the fiber and the nutrients that come attached to it.


We looked at the pairing in more detail in[meal delivery with 40g+ protein and 8g+ fiber](https://www.shoplocale.com/blogs/high-protein/meal-delivery-with-40g-protein-and-8g-fiber) .


## Frequently asked questions


How much fiber do I actually need?


25g a day for women and 38g for men as a baseline. For weight management or blood sugar control, 30g or more with a mix of soluble and insoluble fiber.


Why is fiber so hard to hit?


Because it comes with volume. Reaching 30g means substantial quantities of vegetables, legumes and whole grains, which is a lot of food to prepare and eat when meals are rushed.


Do fiber supplements work as well as food?


They contribute to the total, but isolated fiber lacks the vitamins, minerals and polyphenols that come with whole-food sources. Supplements are a supplement, not a replacement.


Does fiber help with weight loss?


Studies show increasing fiber alone is associated with weight loss, largely through greater fullness and steadier blood sugar rather than any direct effect on fat.


How much fiber is in a Locale meal?


8 grams or more per meal, alongside 40–60g of protein, from whole-food sources.
